bullets: What is inside an atom, how to count its protons, neutrons and electrons, and how electron shells explain the periodic table
slides.heading: Atomic structure and the periodic table
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we look inside the atom, and by the end you will be able to name its three particles, count them for carbon and sodium, draw electron shells, and explain groups and periods.

bullets: Describe the atom: a tiny dense nucleus of protons and neutrons, with electrons in shells around mostly empty space
Count particles from the proton and nucleon numbers, and read groups and periods off the electron arrangement
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud slowly and tell the class: keep these in mind, because our exit ticket will ask you to count particles for an element and to explain what its group and period tell you.

bullets: If the nucleus of an atom were the size of a marble, the atom itself would be about the size of a stadium
So what fills the space between the nucleus and the edge of the atom? Almost nothing - it is empty space
slides.heading: Mostly nothing at all
slides.notes: Ask the class: a model atom looks full and solid, so what is really between the nucleus and the outside? Take two or three answers, then say: hold them, because the answer is almost nothing at all.

bullets: Protons and neutrons sit in the tiny dense nucleus at the centre; electrons sit in fixed shells around it
The proton number fixes the element; the nucleon number is protons plus neutrons; a neutral atom has equal protons and electrons
Shells fill in order: shell 1 holds 2 electrons, shell 2 holds 8, shell 3 holds 8
slides.heading: The atom at a glance
slides.notes: Say this part slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: nearly all the mass is packed into the tiny nucleus, the rest of the atom is mostly empty space, and the electrons sit in fixed shells - they do not circle like planets.

bullets: The nucleus grows at the centre while three shells draw themselves around it - and the space between them stays empty
Electrons drop into their shells one by one: they sit in fixed shells, not in random orbits
slides.heading: Inside the atom
slides.notes: Point at the animation and narrate what is happening: watch the shells appear first, then the tiny nucleus in the middle, then the electrons settling into shell 1. Almost all the mass sits in that tiny nucleus.

bullets: Carbon is element 6: six protons in the nucleus and six electrons around it
Its six electrons fill the shells two, then four - written as 2,4
slides.heading: Counting particles: carbon
slides.notes: Count along with the animation: six protons fix carbon as element 6, and its six electrons fill shell 1 with two and shell 2 with four.

bullets: Sodium is element 11: eleven protons, twelve neutrons and eleven electrons
Its electrons fill two, eight, then one - and that lone outer electron rules sodium's chemistry
slides.heading: Counting particles: sodium
slides.notes: Watch the shells fill: two, then eight, then a single electron alone in shell 3. That lone outer electron is why sodium reacts so fiercely.

bullets: A column of the periodic table is a group: every element in it has the same number of outer electrons
Same outer electrons means similar reactions - that is why group members behave like a family
slides.heading: Groups: the table’s columns
slides.notes: Trace a column of the table as the animation builds it: the outer-electron count repeats down the column, so the chemistry repeats too.

bullets: A row of the periodic table is a period: the period number matches the number of electron shells
Period 2 elements have two shells; period 3 elements have three
slides.heading: Periods: the table’s rows
slides.notes: Follow a row across the table and count the shells as they grow: each new period starts a new outer shell.

bullets: The ball-and-stick model makes atoms look like tiny solid marbles - but the model is a diagram, not the thing itself
Use the shell model, not the planet model: electrons sit in fixed shells around a speck of a nucleus
slides.heading: A common mistake: atoms are solid balls
slides.notes: Name the trap out loud before anyone falls into it: models are drawn solid because that is easy to draw, not because atoms are solid. Watch the nucleus shrink to a speck in the middle of empty space.

bullets: Step 1: sodium has proton number 11 and nucleon number 23, so it has 11 protons, 23 - 11 = 12 neutrons and 11 electrons
Step 2: its electrons arrange as 2,8,1 - three shells means period 3, and one outer electron means group 1
slides.heading: Worked example: read sodium off the table
slides.notes: Talk through the two steps slowly and name each one as you write it; say: first count the particles from the two numbers, then let the electron arrangement tell you the period and the group.

bullets: An element has proton number 8 and nucleon number 16. Count its protons, neutrons and electrons, and write its electron arrangement
Careful - a classmate says an atom is basically a solid marble with electrons stuck on it. Explain to them what is wrong with that picture
slides.heading: Your turn: count and place
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call two pairs: listen for the solid-marble picture. The fix is the shell model: a tiny dense nucleus, electrons in fixed shells, and mostly empty space in between.

bullets: On your own: count the protons, neutrons and electrons in magnesium (proton number 12, nucleon number 24) and write its electron arrangement
Watch out for the trap one last time: picture the atom as mostly empty space with a tiny nucleus, and say where its electrons sit
slides.heading: Exit ticket: prove it before you leave
slides.notes: Close by reminding the class of the trap picture - a solid marble atom - and the fix: a tiny dense nucleus with electrons in fixed shells around mostly empty space. Collect the tickets as they leave and check who can count particles and place the element.
